groups.title: ORM and persistence
groups.mechanism: Hibernate maps object state to relational operations through a persistence context and database integration. Object navigation and SQL execution are different models.
groups.tradeOff: ORM reduces repetitive mapping while making generated queries and lifecycle behavior important to inspect.
groups.verify: Capture SQL for a representative use case and verify committed rows independently.

questions.question: What is an object-relational mapper?
questions.answer: A tool translating between object models and relational storage, including mapping, identity and state-management behavior.

questions.question: When is Hibernate useful?
questions.answer: When entity relationships and managed state suit the domain and its query/transaction behavior can be owned and measured.

questions.question: How does JPA relate to Hibernate?
questions.answer: JPA, now Jakarta Persistence, specifies APIs and contracts; Hibernate ORM is an implementation with additional capabilities.

questions.question: Why is an entity not automatically a good API DTO?
questions.answer: Its lazy relationships, mutable state and persistence metadata can leak internal schema and cause unexpected loading during serialization.

questions.question: How would you choose ORM versus direct SQL?
questions.answer: Compare access patterns, aggregate behavior, query complexity and team ownership; explicit SQL may better fit heavily specialized read workloads.

groups.title: Persistence context
groups.mechanism: The persistence context tracks managed entity identity and state within a lifecycle. It is distinct from a shared second-level cache.
groups.tradeOff: Managed state simplifies updates but can retain large graphs and hide SQL timing.
groups.verify: Load the same row twice in one context, then compare with a separate context.

questions.question: What is the persistence context?
questions.answer: A unit tracking managed entity instances and their lifecycle, providing identity consistency for a persistent identity within that context.

questions.question: When should a context be short-lived?
questions.answer: For request or use-case transactions where bounded retention and clear consistency are preferable to long-lived stale managed graphs.

questions.question: How does first-level caching affect repeated finds?
questions.answer: A managed instance for an identity can be reused within the context, though query execution behavior depends on the operation.

questions.question: Why can a large batch exhaust memory despite small rows?
questions.answer: The context retains managed entities and snapshots until cleared or ended; pending state grows even when individual objects are small.

questions.question: How would you process a large update batch safely?
questions.answer: Use bounded chunks, appropriate flush/clear boundaries and explicit transaction/restart semantics, while measuring SQL batching and retained state.

groups.title: Entity lifecycle
groups.mechanism: Transient, managed, detached and removed describe relationships to a persistence context. State transitions determine dirty tracking and available operations.
groups.tradeOff: Detachment avoids ongoing tracking but requires explicit update and conflict handling.
groups.verify: Exercise persist, detach, merge and remove with an independent verification transaction.

questions.question: What is a transient entity?
questions.answer: An instance not yet associated with a persistence context as a persistent managed entity.

questions.question: When does an entity become detached?
questions.answer: When its association with the context ends or is explicitly removed, leaving an object whose later mutations are not automatically tracked there.

questions.question: What does persist generally do?
questions.answer: It makes a new entity managed and schedules insertion according to identifier strategy, flush rules and transaction behavior.

questions.question: Why do detached changes sometimes never reach the database?
questions.answer: The modified instance is no longer managed and no supported update or merge path was used.

questions.question: How would you design a disconnected edit workflow?
questions.answer: Load authoritative state in a transaction, apply an explicit command, validate version and authorization, and avoid blindly merging arbitrary client object graphs.

groups.title: Merge semantics
groups.mechanism: Merge copies detached state into a managed representation and returns that representation. The original detached instance does not automatically become managed.
groups.tradeOff: Convenient graph copying can overwrite fields that the client never intended to change.
groups.verify: Compare source and returned instances and test missing fields plus stale versions.

questions.question: What does merge return?
questions.answer: A managed instance receiving the supplied state; it may be a different Java object from the detached argument.

questions.question: When is explicit command mapping safer than merge?
questions.answer: For partial client updates or security-sensitive fields, where copying an entire detached graph can overwrite authoritative state.

questions.question: How does merge interact with cascaded associations?
questions.answer: Merge propagation depends on configured cascade semantics and the graph supplied; inspect which related entities can be copied or loaded.

questions.question: Why can using the original instance after merge be wrong?
questions.answer: That object can remain detached, so subsequent changes may not be tracked in the active context.

questions.question: How would you prevent stale detached updates from overwriting newer data?
questions.answer: Use version checks and explicit update semantics, surface conflicts and re-evaluate business decisions from fresh authoritative state.

groups.title: Identifiers
groups.mechanism: Identifier generation determines when identity is assigned and can affect insert timing and batching. Entity identity must remain stable under the mapping contract.
groups.tradeOff: Different generation strategies trade database coordination against batching and portability.
groups.verify: Persist several entities and inspect generated identifiers, insert timing and batch behavior.

questions.question: Why does every entity need an identifier?
questions.answer: The persistence system needs a stable identity to distinguish rows and track managed instances across operations.

questions.question: When is a generated surrogate key useful?
questions.answer: When a stable technical identity should remain separate from mutable or evolving business attributes.

questions.question: How can IDENTITY generation affect insertion batching?
questions.answer: Obtaining generated identifiers can require inserts earlier and restrict batching opportunities; inspect actual Hibernate and database behavior.

questions.question: Why is a mutable natural key a difficult primary identity?
questions.answer: Changes affect references, equality and cache keys; preserve stable identity or explicitly model migration of the business key.

questions.question: How would you choose an identifier strategy for high write throughput?
questions.answer: Compare database support, allocation strategy, ordering, collision guarantees and real batching evidence rather than selecting by annotation convenience.

groups.title: Equality and proxies
groups.mechanism: Entity equality must account for identity assignment and proxy behavior. Reference equality and mutable identifier hashing can break collection membership.
groups.tradeOff: Simple identity rules are safer than broad generated equals methods over associations.
groups.verify: Test transient, managed, detached and proxied forms in sets before and after persistence.

questions.question: Why is entity equality harder than DTO equality?
questions.answer: Entities have lifecycle and identity assignment, and proxies can alter runtime class behavior without changing persistent identity.

questions.question: When should associations be excluded from equals and hashCode?
questions.answer: When traversing them risks recursion, lazy loading or mutable equality; entity identity should not depend on whole mutable graphs.

questions.question: How can a generated ID affect hash-based collections?
questions.answer: If hashCode changes when the identifier is assigned, an entity already stored in a hash collection can become difficult to retrieve.

questions.question: Why can strict getClass equality reject an equivalent proxy?
questions.answer: A proxy can have a different runtime class while representing the same persistent entity; use an intentional proxy-compatible identity strategy.

questions.question: How would you validate an entity equality implementation?
questions.answer: Exercise null IDs, assigned IDs, detached copies, proxies and subclass cases while checking symmetry, stable hashing and collection behavior.

groups.title: Association ownership
groups.mechanism: The owning side controls the relational association update. Inverse-side collections still need in-memory consistency but do not independently own the foreign key.
groups.tradeOff: Convenience navigation increases the need for explicit aggregate update methods.
groups.verify: Modify each side separately and inspect the foreign key after flush.

questions.question: What is the owning side of an association?
questions.answer: The mapped side responsible for writing the relationship's relational representation, such as the foreign key or join table.

questions.question: When should helper methods update both association sides?
questions.answer: When bidirectional navigation is exposed and both references must remain consistent within the application's object graph.

questions.question: What does mappedBy indicate?
questions.answer: That this side is inverse and the relationship is mapped by the named attribute on the owning side.

questions.question: Why can adding to an inverse collection fail to persist the link?
questions.answer: The owning side was not changed, so the relational update required by the mapping was not established.

questions.question: How would you design aggregate association methods?
questions.answer: Centralize add/remove operations, enforce ownership and invariants, and update both sides consistently without exposing uncontrolled collection mutation.

groups.title: Cascades and orphan removal
groups.mechanism: Cascades propagate selected persistence operations; orphan removal models deletion of privately owned children removed from a relationship. Neither means universal recursive business ownership.
groups.tradeOff: Automation reduces boilerplate but can amplify accidental deletes across shared relationships.
groups.verify: Remove one link and inspect which rows are deleted, retained or reassigned.

questions.question: What is a cascade operation?
questions.answer: Propagation of a specified persistence operation from one entity to associated entities according to mapping configuration.

questions.question: When is orphanRemoval appropriate?
questions.answer: For children whose lifecycle is owned by the parent and whose removal from that relationship should delete their persistent state.

questions.question: How does orphanRemoval differ from cascade REMOVE?
questions.answer: Orphan removal responds to relationship orphaning; cascade REMOVE propagates parent removal. Their triggers and ownership implications differ.

questions.question: Why is cascade REMOVE on shared references dangerous?
questions.answer: Deleting one owner can delete an entity still needed by other objects or business processes.

questions.question: How would you review a deletion workflow?
questions.answer: Identify private versus shared ownership, inspect generated deletes and constraints, and test reassignment, missing children and historical references.

groups.title: Fetch strategies
groups.mechanism: Lazy and eager describe fetch requirements rather than a universal SQL shape. Fetch joins, entity graphs and projections must match the use case.
groups.tradeOff: Loading too little creates extra queries; loading too much inflates rows and memory.
groups.verify: Record query count and transferred rows for empty, single and multiple associations.

questions.question: What does lazy fetching defer?
questions.answer: Loading associated state until needed through a supported managed access path, subject to mapping and enhancement capabilities.

questions.question: When is a DTO projection preferable to loading entities?
questions.answer: For read-only endpoints needing a precise subset of fields without managed graph behavior or incidental lazy traversal.

questions.question: Does eager fetching guarantee one SQL query?
questions.answer: No. Required state may be loaded through joins or additional queries depending on mapping, query and provider behavior.

questions.question: Why can lazy access fail outside the context?
questions.answer: The entity lacks an active supported loading mechanism after detachment or session closure.

questions.question: How would you choose a fetch plan for one endpoint?
questions.answer: Specify required data, choose joins or projections deliberately, and verify row multiplication, query count and pagination behavior under realistic cardinality.

groups.title: N+1 and pagination
groups.mechanism: N+1 occurs when loading a set triggers additional per-row queries. Joining multiple collections can instead create a large Cartesian-like row expansion.
groups.tradeOff: Fewer statements do not always mean less work or memory.
groups.verify: Compare statements, rows and latency for realistic parent and child counts.

questions.question: What is an N+1 query pattern?
questions.answer: One query loads many parents, then additional queries load related state separately for each parent or row.

questions.question: When can batch fetching help?
questions.answer: When related lazy state for several owners can be fetched in bounded groups, reducing round trips without one huge join.

questions.question: Why is collection fetch joining with pagination risky?
questions.answer: Row multiplication can distort page semantics or cause in-memory pagination; verify the provider's behavior rather than assuming database limits apply correctly.

questions.question: Why can replacing N+1 with a giant join still be slow?
questions.answer: The join can duplicate parent data across many child combinations, increasing transfer, allocation and result processing.

questions.question: How would you paginate parents with required child data?
questions.answer: Often select a deterministic page of parent identities first, then fetch bounded related data while preserving order and handling concurrent changes.

groups.title: Dirty checking and flush
groups.mechanism: Dirty checking compares managed state and schedules writes. Flush synchronizes pending changes with the database; transaction commit determines durability.
groups.tradeOff: Automatic writes simplify code but make flush timing and state volume important.
groups.verify: Observe SQL before queries, at explicit flush and at commit; verify rollback separately.

questions.question: What is dirty checking?
questions.answer: Detection of changes to managed entity state so Hibernate can generate appropriate updates during synchronization.

questions.question: When is explicit flush useful?
questions.answer: When database constraints or generated effects must be observed before continuing, while remembering that flush is not commit.

questions.question: How does flush differ from commit?
questions.answer: Flush sends pending SQL within the transaction; commit completes the transaction and makes its successful effects durable under database guarantees.

questions.question: Why can a query trigger an unexpected update?
questions.answer: Flush rules may synchronize pending managed changes before executing a query that must observe consistent state.

questions.question: How would you diagnose an unexpected write?
questions.answer: Inspect which managed object changed, cascade paths, flush timing and transaction scope before blaming the final query that exposed the write.

groups.title: Optimistic locking
groups.mechanism: A version predicate lets the database reject updates based on stale state. Detecting a conflict does not decide how the business should resolve it.
groups.tradeOff: Optimistic locking avoids long blocking but may require retries or user-visible conflicts.
groups.verify: Run two writers from the same version and assert one cannot silently overwrite the other.

questions.question: What does Version provide?
questions.answer: Optimistic concurrency checking using a version attribute so stale updates can be detected rather than silently replacing newer state.

questions.question: When is optimistic locking a good fit?
questions.answer: When conflicts are relatively uncommon and the application can handle rejection or retry without holding long-lived database locks.

questions.question: How does an optimistic update detect a conflict?
questions.answer: The update includes the expected version; a mismatch means the row no longer has the state version the writer read.

questions.question: Why is blindly retrying a stale edit unsafe?
questions.answer: The original user decision may no longer be valid against the newer state. Recompute or surface a conflict according to the use case.

questions.question: How would you test a versioned partial update?
questions.answer: Use independent transactions, apply conflicting field changes and verify stale input cannot overwrite newer authorized values or bypass business validation.

groups.title: Pessimistic locking
groups.mechanism: Database locks protect specific rows or ranges under database rules. Locking requires an active transaction and a defined acquisition order plus timeout.
groups.tradeOff: Locks serialize conflicting work but increase waiting and deadlock risk.
groups.verify: Use two connections to test contention, timeout and release on rollback.

questions.question: What is pessimistic locking?
questions.answer: Acquiring database locks to prevent conflicting concurrent operations during a transaction, according to the selected lock mode and database behavior.

questions.question: When is it preferable to optimistic retries?
questions.answer: When contention and expensive conflicting work make controlled serialization more predictable than repeated failed attempts.

questions.question: Does locking an entity automatically lock every related row?
questions.answer: No. Scope depends on the query, lock mode, mapping and database; explicitly identify all rows protecting the invariant.

questions.question: Why can consistent business code still deadlock?
questions.answer: Two transactions can acquire required locks in different orders and wait on each other.

questions.question: How would you prevent lock-induced service exhaustion?
questions.answer: Keep transactions short, order acquisitions consistently, set bounded waits and retry deadlocks safely while monitoring connection and request queues.

groups.title: Transaction and session boundaries
groups.mechanism: A session coordinates persistence state; a transaction coordinates database atomicity. Long session lifetimes can obscure when data is loaded or written.
groups.tradeOff: Convenient lazy access may extend database activity into presentation code.
groups.verify: Inspect SQL across service and response rendering boundaries and test detached use explicitly.

questions.question: How do Session and transaction differ?
questions.answer: A Session manages persistence context operations; a transaction defines a database consistency and completion boundary used by those operations.

questions.question: When should remote calls be kept outside a database transaction?
questions.answer: When their latency and uncertainty would retain locks or connections unnecessarily and no local atomicity benefit covers the external effect.

questions.question: Why is an open-session-in-view policy controversial?
questions.answer: It can permit lazy queries during response rendering, hiding query count and transaction-boundary assumptions in presentation paths.

questions.question: What happens when asynchronous work uses a closed session?
questions.answer: Operations can fail or access detached state; sessions and transaction-bound connections should not be casually shared across threads.

questions.question: How would you define a reliable persistence service boundary?
questions.answer: Load required state, validate and update inside a clear transaction, return explicit DTOs and expose commit or conflict outcomes deliberately.

groups.title: Bulk operations
groups.mechanism: Bulk DML acts directly on database rows and can bypass normal entity-state synchronization and callbacks. Managed instances can become stale afterward.
groups.tradeOff: Bulk operations improve throughput while requiring explicit context and version handling.
groups.verify: Load an entity, run bulk DML and compare managed state with a fresh-context read.

questions.question: When is bulk update useful?
questions.answer: For set-based changes where per-entity loading is unnecessary and the bypassed lifecycle behavior is acceptable.

questions.question: How does bulk DML differ from changing managed entities?
questions.answer: It operates through a query directly and does not provide the same per-instance dirty checking and callback semantics.

questions.question: Why should the persistence context be cleared or refreshed after bulk DML?
questions.answer: Previously managed instances may retain stale values inconsistent with rows changed by the bulk operation.

questions.question: Why can a bulk update undermine optimistic locking?
questions.answer: Version increments and predicates may need explicit handling; do not assume ordinary entity update semantics are automatically reproduced.

questions.question: How would you execute a safe data correction?
questions.answer: Define exact predicates and affected-row expectations, handle version/cache consequences, verify in bounded batches and retain recovery evidence.

groups.title: SQL batching
groups.mechanism: JDBC batching groups compatible statements; transaction chunking and identifier strategies affect what can actually batch. Fetch batching is a different optimization.
groups.tradeOff: Larger batches reduce round trips but increase retained work and failure recovery size.
groups.verify: Observe actual batch execution and verify restart behavior after a mid-batch failure.

questions.question: What is JDBC statement batching?
questions.answer: Sending compatible parameterized statement executions together through the driver to reduce round trips and execution overhead.

questions.question: When do flush and clear help batch processing?
questions.answer: At controlled chunk boundaries to send pending work and release managed-state retention, with a deliberate transaction policy.

questions.question: How does insert ordering affect batching?
questions.answer: Grouping compatible entity statements can increase batch opportunities, but actual benefits depend on constraints and workload.

questions.question: Why does setting batch_size not prove batching occurs?
questions.answer: Identifier generation, statement differences, driver support and flushing behavior can prevent the expected grouping.

questions.question: How would you measure a batch optimization?
questions.answer: Compare round trips, statement batches, transaction duration, memory and failure recovery while confirming identical persisted business results.

groups.title: Caching layers
groups.mechanism: First-level state belongs to a persistence context; second-level and query caches have separate provider and invalidation contracts. External writers can invalidate assumptions.
groups.tradeOff: Shared caching lowers repeated loads but adds stale-data and coordination risks.
groups.verify: Update through a different application path and measure what each cache observes.

questions.question: How does second-level cache differ from first-level cache?
questions.answer: Second-level cache can share mapped entity data across contexts, while first-level identity and managed state belong to one persistence context.

questions.question: When is entity caching appropriate?
questions.answer: For read-heavy data with a suitable consistency and invalidation strategy, not simply every entity in the model.

questions.question: What does a query cache need beyond result reuse?
questions.answer: Correct association with underlying data changes and the provider's invalidation semantics; cached query results are not a universal fresh-data guarantee.

questions.question: Why can direct SQL writers create stale ORM cache entries?
questions.answer: They may bypass the cache invalidation path used by ORM-managed updates.

questions.question: How would you validate a shared cache strategy?
questions.answer: Test concurrent readers/writers, external updates, eviction, provider failure and deployment compatibility under the required freshness contract.

groups.title: Inheritance and mapping choices
groups.mechanism: Inheritance strategies map type hierarchies to different table layouts and query patterns. The object model does not determine the optimal relational representation.
groups.tradeOff: Convenient polymorphism can increase joins, null columns or union complexity.
groups.verify: Inspect generated queries and constraints for each concrete subtype.

questions.question: What are common JPA inheritance strategies?
questions.answer: Single-table, joined and table-per-class mappings, each with different schema and polymorphic query trade-offs.

questions.question: When is an embeddable useful?
questions.answer: For a value-like group of fields owned by an entity rather than requiring an independent persistent identity and lifecycle.

questions.question: How does single-table inheritance affect constraints?
questions.answer: Subtype-specific fields share one table, often complicating required-column rules and increasing nullable columns.

questions.question: Why can joined inheritance slow polymorphic reads?
questions.answer: Retrieving subtype data can require joins across the hierarchy, increasing query complexity and row processing.

questions.question: How would you choose between inheritance and composition in persistence?
questions.answer: Start with domain identity and query patterns, then compare schema constraints, joins, evolution and measured workload rather than mirroring Java inheritance automatically.

groups.title: Queries and parameters
groups.mechanism: JPQL/HQL query entity models; native SQL exposes database-specific capabilities. Bound values prevent injection but dynamic identifiers still need controlled construction.
groups.tradeOff: Abstraction improves portability while complex queries may need explicit dialect-specific SQL.
groups.verify: Test malicious values, empty collections, null predicates and deterministic ordering.

questions.question: How do JPQL and native SQL differ?
questions.answer: JPQL targets mapped entities and attributes; native SQL targets the database schema and can use vendor-specific features.

questions.question: When should a query use bound parameters?
questions.answer: For external values and dynamic data rather than string concatenation, preserving typing and preventing value-based injection.

questions.question: Can a parameter safely replace an arbitrary table name?
questions.answer: Ordinary value parameters do not bind SQL identifiers. Choose identifiers from trusted fixed mappings instead of accepting arbitrary text.

questions.question: Why do empty IN collections need deliberate handling?
questions.answer: Their SQL translation and semantics can vary; define whether empty input means no matches or omitted filtering and test that contract.

questions.question: How would you review a query exposed through sorting options?
questions.answer: Allowlist supported sort fields and directions, bind values, enforce tenant predicates and add a unique tie-breaker for stable pagination.

groups.title: Diagnosis and upgrades
groups.mechanism: ORM incidents require examining generated SQL, context lifetime and the actual database plan. Upgrades can alter query generation or mapping validation without source changes.
groups.tradeOff: Detailed SQL diagnostics can add overhead and expose sensitive values.
groups.verify: Capture representative SQL safely, compare plans and replay real boundary cases across versions.

questions.question: Where should an ORM performance investigation start?
questions.answer: With exact generated statements, query count, transferred rows, database waits and transaction boundaries for the slow use case.

questions.question: When is Hibernate statistics useful?
questions.answer: For controlled visibility into operations such as query execution and cache behavior, while accounting for overhead and interpreting the right scope.

questions.question: How can an upgrade break a previously accepted mapping?
questions.answer: Validation, SQL generation, type handling or specification alignment can become stricter or behave differently across supported versions.

questions.question: Why is compiling entities insufficient upgrade validation?
questions.answer: It does not exercise mapping bootstrap, schema compatibility, lazy loading, query generation or concurrent transaction behavior.

questions.question: How would you validate a Hibernate migration?
questions.answer: Bootstrap all mappings, run target-database integration tests, compare generated SQL and verify equality, locking, pagination and rollback-sensitive workflows.

groups.title: @Entity, @Table and access strategy
groups.mechanism: Hibernate reads entity mapping metadata during bootstrap. Identifier placement influences default field or property access, and explicit Access can override that choice.
groups.tradeOff: Annotations reduce mapping files but inconsistent access can silently change which state is persisted.
groups.verify: Bootstrap mappings and verify round trips for fields with deliberately different accessor behavior.

questions.question: What does @Entity cause Hibernate to recognize?
questions.answer: A managed persistent type in the persistence unit's discovered mapping set; the annotation does not itself register every class globally.

questions.question: How does @Table differ from @Entity?
questions.answer: Entity identifies a persistence model type; Table specifies relational table mapping details rather than creating ordinary application instances.

questions.question: How can @Id placement affect access strategy?
questions.answer: Placing mapping annotations on fields or getters establishes default field or property access under persistence rules unless explicitly overridden.

questions.question: Why can annotating the wrong member leave a value unmapped?
questions.answer: The active access strategy may inspect a different member path, so inconsistent placement can produce unexpected mapping behavior.

questions.question: How would you review mapping discovery and access?
questions.answer: Inspect persistence-unit discovery, access strategy and mapped attributes, then verify actual stored values rather than only schema generation.

groups.title: @Id and @GeneratedValue internals
groups.mechanism: Identifier metadata selects how persistent identity is assigned. Hibernate coordinates generator behavior with database capabilities, allocation and insert execution.
groups.tradeOff: Generation convenience can affect batching, ordering and portability.
groups.verify: Persist multiple new entities and inspect allocation, inserts and assigned identities.

questions.question: What does @Id identify?
questions.answer: The entity attribute or supported composite structure representing persistent identity within the mapping.

questions.question: How does @GeneratedValue influence persistence?
questions.answer: It selects a supported identifier-generation strategy whose runtime behavior depends on provider and database integration.

questions.question: Why can @SequenceGenerator allocationSize matter?
questions.answer: It affects identifier allocation coordination and performance; align its use with the database sequence and provider's expected strategy.

questions.question: Why can assuming identifiers are consecutive fail?
questions.answer: Allocation, rollback, caching and concurrency can leave gaps. Identity uniqueness is not a gap-free business numbering contract.

questions.question: How would you choose an annotation-based ID strategy?
questions.answer: Check database support, throughput, batching, migration compatibility and equality behavior before and after identity assignment.

groups.title: @Column, @Basic and @Transient
groups.mechanism: Mapping annotations describe persistence representation. Database constraints, validation annotations and Java memory visibility are distinct mechanisms despite similar terms.
groups.tradeOff: Schema metadata helps documentation but deployed schema must be checked independently.
groups.verify: Attempt invalid writes against the migrated database and inspect what is actually stored.

questions.question: What does @Column(nullable=false) express?
questions.answer: Column mapping/schema-generation metadata; enforce the intended deployed database constraint and validation rather than assuming every path rejects null early.

questions.question: How does persistence @Transient differ from Java transient?
questions.answer: The annotation excludes a member from persistence mapping; the Java modifier affects serialization and can interact with field mapping rules differently.

questions.question: Does @Column(length=...) validate every Java string assignment?
questions.answer: No. It supplies mapping metadata; runtime validation and database enforcement depend on configured validation plus actual schema.

questions.question: Why can a schema and annotation disagree?
questions.answer: Production migrations, historical tables or disabled schema generation can differ from source mapping declarations.

questions.question: How would you enforce a required bounded text field?
questions.answer: Align Bean Validation, explicit application rules and database constraints, then test writes through all supported paths.

groups.title: @OneToMany, @ManyToOne and @JoinColumn
groups.mechanism: Association metadata describes ownership, join columns, fetch and cascade behavior. The relational writer is the owning side; inverse collections do not own the foreign key.
groups.tradeOff: Rich navigation is useful while uncontrolled graph traversal causes hidden queries and mutation complexity.
groups.verify: Modify each side independently and verify foreign-key updates plus query counts.

questions.question: How does @ManyToOne map a common foreign-key relationship?
questions.answer: The referencing entity holds association metadata pointing to the target identity, commonly through a JoinColumn on the owning side.

questions.question: What does mappedBy on @OneToMany mean internally?
questions.answer: It identifies the owning attribute on the other entity so this collection is inverse rather than an independent foreign-key writer.

questions.question: How do fetch and cascade settings differ?
questions.answer: Fetch describes loading requirements; cascade describes propagation of persistence operations. Neither substitutes for the other.

questions.question: Why does adding only to a mappedBy collection sometimes do nothing?
questions.answer: The owning association was not updated, so the required foreign-key change was not established.

questions.question: How would you make a bidirectional mapping robust?
questions.answer: Provide aggregate methods updating both sides, choose narrow cascades and test add, remove, reassignment and detached cases.

groups.title: @OneToOne and @MapsId
groups.mechanism: One-to-one mappings require relational uniqueness and explicit ownership. Shared-primary-key associations tie dependent identity to the owner through supported MapsId semantics.
groups.tradeOff: Shared identity models private dependents well but constrains independent lifecycle and reassignment.
groups.verify: Test absent dependents, uniqueness conflicts and owner/dependent insert order.

questions.question: What does @OneToOne promise conceptually?
questions.answer: A single associated entity at each side's mapped cardinality, which should be supported by appropriate relational constraints.

questions.question: When is @MapsId useful?
questions.answer: When a dependent entity's identity derives from an associated owner's identity under a shared or derived identifier mapping.

questions.question: Why does optional=false not replace a database constraint?
questions.answer: Mapping assumptions and actual storage enforcement differ; external writers and historical data still require relational integrity.

questions.question: Why can one-to-one lazy loading behave differently from expectations?
questions.answer: Ownership, optionality and provider enhancement capabilities can affect whether association presence or state requires a query.

questions.question: How would you validate a dependent-entity lifecycle?
questions.answer: Persist, remove and reload both sides across separate contexts, verifying identity, nullability, uniqueness and private-ownership rules.

groups.title: @Version and lock annotations
groups.mechanism: Version metadata participates in update predicates to detect stale writes. Lock modes influence database locking but remain dependent on query and transaction context.
groups.tradeOff: Conflicts protect data but must become meaningful application outcomes.
groups.verify: Run competing writers and inspect affected-row/version behavior plus rollback.

questions.question: How does @Version protect an update internally?
questions.answer: Hibernate includes the expected version in the database update contract and detects a mismatch when the stored version changed.

questions.question: When should a stale version be returned as a conflict?
questions.answer: When the caller's edit depends on the state it read and automatic recomputation would change the intended decision.

questions.question: Does @Version automatically coordinate external side effects?
questions.answer: No. It protects participating entity updates, while remote writes and event publication require separate consistency design.

questions.question: Why can a bulk update bypass ordinary version behavior?
questions.answer: Bulk DML does not necessarily reproduce managed-entity update processing; explicit version logic and context synchronization may be required.

questions.question: How would you verify optimistic-lock annotations after migration?
questions.answer: Use separate transactions and detached copies, assert one stale write fails and check that no external irreversible effect was repeated during recovery.

groups.title: @Enumerated, @Convert and value mappings
groups.mechanism: Enum and converter metadata define translation between Java values and database representation. Persisted codes must remain stable across deployments.
groups.tradeOff: Automatic conversion reduces repetition while hiding compatibility hazards in historical data.
groups.verify: Round-trip null, unknown historical codes and every supported current alternative.

questions.question: Why choose EnumType.STRING over ORDINAL in many models?
questions.answer: Names are usually less sensitive to reordering than ordinals, although renaming constants still requires an explicit persisted-data migration.

questions.question: What does @Converter do?
questions.answer: It declares a supported attribute converter translating between entity attribute and database representation under configured application rules.

questions.question: How does autoApply change converter scope?
questions.answer: It can apply conversion to eligible matching attributes without each explicit Convert declaration, increasing the importance of scope review.

questions.question: Why can a converter break old rows after deployment?
questions.answer: It may reject or reinterpret historical values, even though all newly written examples round-trip successfully.

questions.question: How would you evolve a converted value type?
questions.answer: Define stable persisted codes and tolerant historical reading, migrate data deliberately and test both old and new representations before removing compatibility.

groups.title: @NamedEntityGraph and query mapping annotations
groups.mechanism: NamedEntityGraph declares named attribute-graph metadata. An application selects a graph through supported fetch/load hints or APIs; declaration alone does not apply it to every query. NamedQuery separately declares a reusable query definition.
groups.tradeOff: Reusable declarations aid consistency but query shape and data volume still determine cost.
groups.verify: Capture SQL and result completeness for empty, single and multiple related rows.

questions.question: What does @NamedQuery declare?
questions.answer: A named entity-model query available through persistence APIs, with provider validation and runtime execution under the active mapping model.

questions.question: How does @NamedEntityGraph influence loading?
questions.answer: It declares named graph metadata that can be selected through supported fetch/load hints or APIs. Merely declaring the graph does not change every query automatically.

questions.question: Does a graph guarantee one SQL statement?
questions.answer: No. The provider and mapping determine how required state is obtained; inspect actual statements and transferred rows.

questions.question: Why can a reusable fetch graph hurt a paginated endpoint?
questions.answer: Fetching collections can multiply rows or force expensive handling, even when the graph is appropriate for a single-entity view.

questions.question: How would you choose annotation-based versus explicit query fetch plans?
questions.answer: Keep reusable declarations focused, use projections where suitable and validate each endpoint's ordering, pagination and query cost independently.
